original_question: Let V = direct sum_{i >= 0} V_i be a graded vector space and let D be a graded linear operator with D(V_0) = {0}. Is it always possible to define an associative bilinear product with identity on V making V into a graded algebra for which D is a derivation, so that D(ab) = D(a)b + aD(b)?
target_in_paper: Problem 45 in Section 2, "Problems of 2025," which explicitly cites Fomin 1994, Section 2.3. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core existence problem: given a graded vector space and a linear operator D, ask whether one can put an associative bilinear product with identity on the same underlying graded space so that D becomes a derivation satisfying D(ab)=D(a)b+aD(b). That is essentially the substance of Problem 45. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))
missing_details: The ground field is missing. In the cited source context, the ambient object is a graded associative K-algebra with identity, so the bilinearity should be over a field K. ([studylib.net](https://studylib.net/doc/10959445/journal-of-algebraic-combinatorics-3--1994---357-404))

The grading must be made explicit as an N-grading V = ⊕_{n>=0} V_n. Problem 45 is written with nonnegative degrees, not an arbitrary Z-grading. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))

The crucial degree condition on D is missing. In Fomin's Section 2.3, the intended hypothesis is that D lowers degree by 1, i.e. D(V_n) ⊆ V_{n-1} for n>=1 and D(V_0)=0. The notebook's OCR/rendering garbles this point, but the cited source makes the intended condition clear. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))

The question should state that the desired multiplication is a graded product, namely V_i V_j ⊆ V_{i+j}. Saying only graded algebra without spelling this out leaves the stand-alone formulation incomplete. ([studylib.net](https://studylib.net/doc/10959445/journal-of-algebraic-combinatorics-3--1994---357-404))

The unit should be identified as a degree-0 element, i.e. 1 in V_0. This is implicit in the graded-unital algebra language but should be stated in a stand-alone question. ([studylib.net](https://studylib.net/doc/10959445/journal-of-algebraic-combinatorics-3--1994---357-404))

The universal quantifier should be explicit: the question is whether every pair (V,D) with these hypotheses admits such an associative unital graded algebra structure. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))

The motivation from Fomin's construction involves additional data, namely a degree-1 element t with D(t)=r·1, but Problem 45 itself does not ask for that as part of the formal existence question. A faithful rewrite should therefore not build that extra requirement into the main question. ([studylib.net](https://studylib.net/doc/10959445/journal-of-algebraic-combinatorics-3--1994---357-404))
refined_question: Let K be a field, let V = ⊕_{n>=0} V_n be an N-graded K-vector space, and let D:V→V be a K-linear map of degree -1, meaning that D(V_0)=0 and D(V_n)⊆V_{n-1} for every n>=1. Must there exist an associative K-bilinear product V×V→V and a unit 1 in V_0 such that V becomes a unital graded K-algebra with V_i V_j⊆V_{i+j} for all i,j>=0, and such that D is a derivation of this algebra, i.e. D(ab)=D(a)b+aD(b) for all a,b in V?
justification: The draft is targeting Problem 45 almost verbatim, but it omits the most important hidden hypothesis from the cited source context: D is supposed to lower degree by one. Fomin's Section 2.3 supplies the intended ambient setup—graded associative K-algebra with identity, derivation D:A_n→A_{n-1}—while Worley's Problem 45 asks whether, starting only from the graded vector space and such an operator D, one can always manufacture an associative unital graded algebra structure making D a derivation. Because the notebook states this as an open problem, not as a theorem or conjecture with an equivalent reformulation, the sharp paper-faithful rewrite is the direct existence question above and not a stronger variant involving extra elements such as t with D(t)=r·1. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))
